attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post, stated as his belief.

semantics.note: 'I believe' plus 'will' is a firm expectation, so this is a scored forecast. The proposition keeps the three-quarter window and the revenue-savaging consequence.

contract.note: The contract requires first proving, on its own, that AI failed to 'prove itself', but it gives no test for that. It also leaves the revenue lag open-ended, so the claim can never be scored. The plain reading is a firm prediction that an AI collapse would hit big-tech revenues soon after about end-2024. Reading it as a conditional stretches it in the speaker's favour.

evidence.note: Microsoft's own disclosure: revenue up 12% in the quarter ending 2024-12-31. That quarter falls inside the proving window, not the aftermath. One company only.
Alphabet's own disclosure: Q4 2024 revenue up 12%. Same limits: it covers the window's end, not the later aftermath, and it is not a full company basket.

reviews.rationale: The three-quarter window ended at end-2024. Under the contract, the antecedent cannot be established, so the claim cannot be scored. Under a plain reading, the packet has only Q4 2024 growth at two named firms. That quarter is inside the window, and there is no revenue data from the later aftermath. The evidence does not settle whether big-tech revenues were savaged.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: The proposition keeps the 'once usage drops' antecedent and both consequences: falling revenue and unused data-center acres. No deadline was given.

contract.note: Requiring a broad usage decline before the consequences is a fair reading. The contract narrows 'revenue' to AI-related revenue, though the revised proposition rejects that narrowing. This only matters once the antecedent holds, and it does not affect the result here.

evidence.note: Fed note: generative-AI adoption rose through November 2025. This weighs against the antecedent but does not measure usage intensity.
Consumer survey reported by TechRadar: heavy chatbot use fell and non-use rose. Narrow population, unclear methods; it does not show a broad usage decline.
CBRE: primary-market vacancy was 1.4% in H1 2026. This is capacity context only; no usage contraction preceded it.

reviews.rationale: This is a conditional forecast with no deadline. The packet does not establish a broad decline in AI usage. Adoption measures rose, and one narrow consumer survey shows a decline. With the antecedent unknown, the consequences cannot be scored.

attribution.note: Zitron's own assertion in his own post.

semantics.note: This captures the core assertion that OpenAI's pace of capability progress had slowed. The executives'-futures framing and the GPT-4 admission are separate, secondary points.

contract.note: Reading 'slowed' as smaller broad gains per unit of time is ordinary. The baseline window was chosen by the evaluator because the speaker gave none, so the result depends on that choice.

evidence.note: OpenAI's own disclosure: some tasks may get worse, though most metrics improved. This confirms the admission but does not measure the overall rate of progress.
Preprint comparing March and June 2023 snapshots: mixed regressions and gains. It does not measure the broad rate of improvement.
OpenAI's own disclosure of later improvements in November 2023. Improvement alone does not show whether the pace slowed or not.

reviews.rationale: No item gives a consistent, broad capability time series across the earlier and later periods. The evidence shows task-level regressions and some improvements, which settles neither a slowdown nor a steady pace.
